html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. TTL: time to live; MCP: Model Context Protocol

  • The context window as a budget and how to stay inside it
  • Context engineering techniques: pruning, compaction, isolation, external memory
  • Prompt caching: rules, ordering and savings
  • Modular prompts and Skills (progressive disclosure)
  • Token optimization levers and measurement

2The Context Is a Budget

Running case

Lumen Advisory and the Retail Client's Slow, Costly Assistant

  • A retailer's assistant sends a 12,000-token policy and catalog extract on every request, plus the full chat history
  • By the afternoon, answers drift and the bill is three times the forecast
  • Everything in the window competes: system prompt, tools, history, documents, tool results. More is not better; relevant and well ordered is better.
  • The API is stateless: you resend what the model needs. Tokens are billed as input and output; thinking tokens bill as output.
  • Context drift and bloat raise cost and latency and lower quality.
  • Use token counting (an estimate endpoint) to plan prompts, route models and fit budgets.

Technique What it does Use when
Prune tool output Keep only fields the next step needs Tools return verbose records
Compaction Replace older turns with a summary (server-side or your own call) Long conversations near the limit
Context editing Clear old tool results automatically Agent loops with big results
Isolation Do verbose work in a subagent; return a summary Exploration would flood the main window
External memory Store facts in files or a store; load when relevant (memory tool) Facts must outlive the window
Just-in-time retrieval Fetch documents when needed Large corpora (Module 9)
Ordering Long documents first; question and instructions last Long-context prompts
  • Compaction can lose exact figures and commitments: keep them in a persistent block resent each turn.
  • A 1M-token window does not remove the need for retrieval on very large corpora, and long contexts cost more and can dilute attention.

3Prompt Caching

Rule Detail
Prefix order Tools, then system, then messages; the cache covers the exact prefix up to a breakpoint
Breakpoints Automatic caching with one top-level cache_control, or explicit breakpoints (at most 4)
TTL 5 minutes (default) or 1 hour; refreshed when the entry is read
Minimum About 512 tokens on current tiers; shorter prompts run without caching and without an error
Price Reads are a fraction of base input (10%; 5% or 2.5% on some tiers); writes 1.25x (5 min) or 2x (1 hour)
Invalidation Any change in the prefix (a timestamp, a reordered tool, a different tool set) breaks the match
Check usage fields cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens
  • Stable content first, dynamic last. Never put timestamps, user names or random IDs before the cached text.
  • Keep tool definitions stable (deferred tool loading preserves the prefix; Module 7).
  • Caching reduces latency and cost together; it helps only when the same prefix repeats within the TTL.
  • It also makes contextual retrieval and large few-shot blocks cheap to reuse (Module 9).
Exam tip

For a long, repeated static prompt with a short varying question, the best single optimization is caching the stable prefix (static first). Truncating needed context or shrinking the model blindly are the distractors.

4Modular Prompts and Skills

  • Modular prompts: compose a prompt from versioned blocks (safety, tone, task, schema, tool guidance). Shared blocks keep many assistants consistent.
  • Skills package procedures, scripts and reference files that Claude loads only when relevant.
Level Loaded Cost
Metadata (name, description) Always, in the system prompt Small
SKILL.md instructions When the skill triggers Moderate
Resources and scripts As needed; scripts run without their code entering the context Only when used

  • Use a Skill for a repeatable procedure (report format, review checklist); use a Project or knowledge store for background; use MCP for live data and actions.
  • Write precise descriptions (they decide when a skill triggers).

5Token Optimization Levers

Lever Effect
Cache the prefix Cuts input cost and time-to-first-token on repeats
Shorter prompts and examples Fewer input tokens
Ask for concise output; set max_tokens Fewer output tokens (blunt cap cuts mid-sentence)
Structured output Short, parseable answers
Route to smaller tiers Lower price per token
Batch API 50% off for non-urgent work
Prune, compact, isolate Smaller context per turn
Lower effort Fewer thinking tokens
  • Measure first (token counts, cache hit rate, cost per request) before optimizing (Module 12).
Exam tip

Any change before the cache breakpoint (a timestamp, a reordered tool) breaks the cache; put variable text after the stable prefix.

Exam tip

Compaction can lose exact figures: keep numbers and commitments in a persistent block.

6Exam Q&A

S1An assistant resends a 12,000-token catalog extract with every request, followed by a short user message. Which change cuts cost and latency most directly?

  • AMove to the smallest tier regardless of quality
  • BPlace the catalog before the user message and enable prompt caching on that stable prefix
  • CReduce the catalog to its first section regardless of the question
  • DConvert the catalog into few-shot examples placed after the user message so that it is repeated each time
Show the answer

Answer: B. A repeated stable prefix is what caching reuses.

S2Cache hits stopped after a developer added the current time to the start of the system prompt. Why?

  • AThe model now ignores cached content
  • BThe cache TTL was reduced by the change, so entries now expire before the next request arrives
  • CTimestamps are not allowed in prompts
  • DA changing value at the start of the prefix invalidates the exact-prefix match
Show the answer

Answer: D. Any change in the prefix breaks the cache; put variable text after it.

S3A conversation nears the context limit and must keep exact contract numbers. What is the best approach?

  • ASummarize everything into one paragraph and discard the originals so that the context is as short as possible
  • BSwitch to the largest model so that nothing needs to be dropped, whatever the cost per request
  • CDrop the oldest turns without replacement
  • DCompact older turns, but keep the exact figures in a persistent block resent each turn
Show the answer

Answer: D. Summaries can lose exact values; protect them separately.

S4Which TWO describe how Skills reduce context cost? Select TWO.

  • AOnly metadata is always loaded; instructions load when the skill triggers
  • BAll skill files are loaded into every conversation up front
  • CSkills replace the system prompt entirely
  • DSkills remove the need for descriptions
  • EScripts can run without their source code entering the context
Show the answer

Answer: A, E. Progressive disclosure keeps most content out of the window until needed.

S5A prompt of 300 tokens is sent with cache_control. No caching occurs and no error is returned. What is the likely reason?

  • AThe API silently disabled caching for the account because the prompt contained a cache_control field
  • BCaching requires streaming to be enabled
  • CShort prompts are cached only for one second
  • DThe prompt is below the minimum cacheable length, so it is processed without caching
Show the answer

Answer: D. Prompts under the minimum run uncached without an error; check the usage fields.

S6Which action is most likely to improve both latency and cost for repetitive long prompts?

  • ARaising effort to maximum
  • BDoubling the number of few-shot examples so that the model has more material to reuse each time
  • CCaching a stable prefix and keeping dynamic text after it
  • DDisabling streaming
Show the answer

Answer: C. Reuse of the static prefix reduces processing time and price.

S7A subagent explores 200 files to answer a question. How should its results reach the lead agent?

  • ABy writing them into the system prompt of the lead so that the lead can reread them on every turn
  • BAs a concise summary, keeping the raw exploration in the subagent's own context
  • CAs the full transcript so that nothing is lost
  • DAs an unstructured paste of all file contents
Show the answer

Answer: B. Returning a concise summary keeps the subagent's raw exploration out of the lead's window and the lead's context small.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Context A budget; stateless API; thinking bills as output
Techniques Prune · compact · edit · isolate · external memory · just-in-time retrieval
Cache Static first; prefix exact; max 4 breakpoints; 5 min or 1 hour; about 512 minimum
Savings Reads 10% (5% / 2.5% some tiers); writes 1.25x / 2x
Break Any change in the prefix
Skills Metadata always; instructions on trigger; resources on demand
Tokens Cache, trim, concise output, route, batch, lower effort; measure first
